content.title: Increasing, Decreasing, and Critical Points
content.overview: This lesson focuses on using the first derivative to determine the monotonicity of a function and to identify and classify local extrema. By analyzing the sign of the derivative, we can determine where a function is increasing or decreasing and apply the First Derivative Test to find local maxima and minima.
learning_objectives: Identify critical points where the derivative is zero or undefined.
Determine intervals of increase and decrease using the sign of the first derivative.
Apply the First Derivative Test to classify local extrema.
Justify the behavior of a function based on the sign of its derivative.

sections.title: Monotonicity and the First Derivative
sections.content: The monotonicity of a function refers to whether it is increasing or decreasing. According to the Mean Value Theorem, if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b): 1. If f'(x) > 0 for all x in (a, b), then f is strictly increasing on [a, b]. 2. If f'(x) < 0 for all x in (a, b), then f is strictly decreasing on [a, b]. To find these intervals, we first identify critical points—values of x in the domain of f where f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) is undefined.

sections.title: The First Derivative Test
sections.content: The First Derivative Test is used to classify critical points as local maxima, local minima, or neither. Suppose c is a critical point of a continuous function f: 1. Local Maximum: If f'(x) changes from positive to negative at x = c, then f has a local maximum at c. 2. Local Minimum: If f'(x) changes from negative to positive at x = c, then f has a local minimum at c. 3. No Extrema: If f'(x) does not change sign at x = c (e.g., stays positive on both sides), then f has no local extremum at c.

sections.title: The Sign-Chart Sweep Strategy
sections.content:
To systematically analyze a function: 1. Find f'(x). 2. Determine all critical points (f'(x) = 0 or undefined) and note the domain endpoints. 3. Create a sign chart by picking test values in each subinterval created by the critical points. 4. Evaluate the sign of f' at each test value. 5. Interpret the results: '+' means increasing, '-' means decreasing. 6. Identify sign changes to locate extrema.

![A flow chart showing the steps: Find f'(x), Identify Critical Points, Test Interval Signs, and Apply First Derivative Test.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/b1edf956-3a74-4bf4-9690-eb6e0dac27c3-1786519359017-148.webp)

worked_examples.question: Let f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 2 be defined on the interval [0, 6]. Determine the intervals where f is increasing or decreasing and classify all local extrema.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Find the derivative. f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9. Step 2: Find critical points by setting f'(x) = 0. 3(x^2 - 4x + 3) = 0 => 3(x - 1)(x - 3) = 0. The critical points are x = 1 and x = 3. Step 3: Test signs on intervals (0, 1), (1, 3), and (3, 6). For x = 0.5, f'(0.5) = 3(0.5-1)(0.5-3) = 3(-0.5)(-2.5) = 3.75 (> 0). For x = 2, f'(2) = 3(2-1)(2-3) = 3(1)(-1) = -3 (< 0). For x = 4, f'(4) = 3(4-1)(4-3) = 3(3)(1) = 9 (> 0). Step 4: Conclusion. f increases on [0, 1) and (3, 6] because f' > 0. f decreases on (1, 3) because f' < 0. Step 5: Classify extrema. At x = 1, f' changes from + to -, so there is a local maximum at (1, 6). At x = 3, f' changes from - to +, so there is a local minimum at (3, 2).

common_mistakes: Forgetting to check where the derivative is undefined; critical points are not just where f'(x) = 0.
Confusing the sign of f(x) with the sign of f'(x). Only the sign of f'(x) determines if f is increasing or decreasing.
Assuming a critical point must be an extremum. If f'(x) = x^2, x = 0 is a critical point but not an extremum because the sign does not change.
Swapping the conditions for max and min (e.g., thinking + to - is a minimum).
exam_tips: Always state the reason for an extremum using the sign change of f'. Example: 'f has a local maximum at x=c because f' changes from positive to negative at x=c.'
Check the domain. If a point is not in the domain of the original function, it cannot be a local extremum even if the derivative is zero there.
On the AP exam, a sign chart is a great scratchpad tool but is usually not sufficient as a standalone justification; write out the conclusion in sentences.
content.recap: To find where a function increases or decreases, find the critical points where f' is zero or undefined. Use a sign chart to determine the sign of f' on the resulting intervals. A positive derivative indicates an increasing function, while a negative derivative indicates a decreasing function. Local extrema occur only at critical points where the derivative changes sign.

knowledge_claims.content: A critical point of a function f is a value x in the domain of f where f'(x) is equal to zero or f'(x) is undefined.
If f'(x) > 0 for all x in an interval, then the function f is strictly increasing on that interval.
If f'(x) < 0 for all x in an interval, then the function f is strictly decreasing on that interval.
To find intervals of monotonicity, one must solve f'(x) = 0 and identify where f'(x) is undefined to establish test intervals.
According to the First Derivative Test, a local maximum occurs at a critical point c if f'(x) changes from positive to negative at x = c.
According to the First Derivative Test, a local minimum occurs at a critical point c if f'(x) changes from negative to positive at x = c.
If the derivative f'(x) does not change sign at a critical point, that point is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum.
It is a misconception that all critical points are local extrema; an extremum only exists if the first derivative changes sign.
When classifying extrema, one must verify that the critical point is actually within the domain of the original function f.
To justify a local minimum on the AP exam, you must explicitly state that f' changes from negative to positive at that specific x-value.
While f'(x) = 0 identifies horizontal tangents, critical points where f'(x) is undefined often correspond to sharp corners or vertical tangents in the graph of f.
The sign of the derivative on an interval can be determined by evaluating f' at a single test value within that interval, provided no critical points exist inside it.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Increasing, Decreasing, and Critical Points — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Increasing, Decreasing, and Critical Points: The sign of the first derivative determines intervals of increase and decrease and helps classify local extrema at critical points.
options.B: Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions: Integration by parts reverses the product rule, while partial fractions decomposes rational functions into simpler integrable terms.
options.C: Average Value and Net Change: The average value of a function divides its integral by interval length, while net change integrates a rate with signs preserved.
options.D: Arc Length of Parametric and Vector Curves: Arc length accumulates speed, using the square root of the sum of squared component derivatives.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because The sign of the first derivative determines intervals of increase and decrease and helps classify local extrema at critical points. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Increasing, Decreasing, and Critical Points — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Improper Integrals: An improper integral is defined by a limit at an infinite bound or unbounded integrand and converges only when that limit is finite.
options.B: Increasing, Decreasing, and Critical Points: The sign of the first derivative determines intervals of increase and decrease and helps classify local extrema at critical points.
options.C: Area Between Curves: Area between curves integrates top minus bottom or right minus left after locating relevant intersections and interval changes.
options.D: Polar Coordinates and Derivatives: Polar points use radius and angle, and polar slope follows from parametric differentiation of x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta.
